why.keyToCount: {{key}} has {{answer}}. Count along the circle of fifths from C (no accidentals).
why.lastSharp: The last sharp is the leading tone — a half step below the tonic. {{key}}: {{answer}}.
why.penultimateFlat: The second-to-last flat names the key. {{key}}: {{answer}}.
why.singleFlat: {{key}} has just one flat: {{answer}}. The second-to-last-flat rule needs at least two flats, so learn this one by heart.
why.sigToKey: {{sig}} belongs to {{answer}} — read the signature off the circle of fifths.
why.relative: Relative keys share a key signature, a minor third apart. {{key}}: {{answer}}.
why.circleOrder: Sharps are added F C G D A E B; flats reverse it B E A D G C F. Each step is a perfect fifth.
why.intervalLetterFirst: Count letters first, then set the quality by half steps. The answer is {{answer}}.
why.semitoneFact_one: A recognition fact: the {{answer}} spans {{n}} semitone. Never spell by counting semitones — letters first.
why.semitoneFact_other: A recognition fact: the {{answer}} spans {{n}} semitones. Never spell by counting semitones — letters first.
why.scaleKeySig: The {{scale}} scale uses its key signature: {{accs}}.
why.scaleNoAccidentals: The {{scale}} scale has no sharps or flats.
why.scaleDegree: The {{scale}} scale is {{notes}}, so degree {{num}} is {{answer}}. Key signature: {{accs}}.
why.scaleDegreeNoAccidentals: The {{scale}} scale is {{notes}}, so degree {{num}} is {{answer}}. No sharps or flats.
why.harmonicRaise: The {{scale}} scale raises {{raised}} relative to the natural minor.
why.seventhLadder: Build from the major 7th, then {{step}}. That gives {{chord}}.
why.diatonicMember: {{chord}} is the diatonic chord built on that degree of {{key}}.
why.notDiatonic: {{chord}} is not diatonic in {{key}}: it needs a note from outside the key. The diatonic triad on that root is {{diatonic}} ({{numeral}}).
why.romanPattern: In any {{mode}} key, the triad on degree {{num}} is {{chord}} — the quality pattern never changes.
why.romanPatternNaturalMinor: In natural minor, the triad on degree {{num}} is {{chord}}. Raising the 7th (harmonic minor) changes the triads on degrees 3, 5 and 7.
why.functionPull: {{chord}} pulls {{direction}} — that is its harmonic function.
why.cadencePerfect: {{answer}} (UK: {{uk}}): V → I with both chords in root position and the tonic in the top voice. Invert either chord, or end the top voice on another note, and it becomes an imperfect authentic cadence.
why.v7Derivation: Degree 5 of {{key}} is {{five}}; its dominant seventh is {{answer}}.
why.readPlaces: Written {{written}} sounds {{sounding}}: the guitar sounds an octave lower than written. {{places}} (circled number = string, then the fret).

lesson.nudgeNoteId: Count from a note you know — {{ref}} — one letter for each line or space, up or down to this note.
lesson.nudgeRefTrebleG: the G on the second line, the line the treble clef curls around
lesson.nudgeRefTrebleE: the E on the bottom line
lesson.nudgeRefTrebleF: the F on the top line
lesson.nudgeRefTrebleC: middle C, on the ledger line just below the staff
lesson.nudgeRefBassF: the F on the fourth line, the line between the bass clef's two dots
lesson.nudgeRefBassG: the G on the bottom line
lesson.nudgeRefBassA: the A on the top line
lesson.nudgeRefBassC: middle C, on the ledger line just above the staff
lesson.nudgeChord: Count up from the root: the other notes lie {{intervals}} above it.
lesson.nudgeScale: The steps from the first note up: {{steps}} (W = whole step, H = half step).
lesson.nudgeScaleWide: The steps from the first note up: {{steps}} (W = whole step, H = half step, W+H = a step and a half).
lesson.nudgeInterval: Count the letters from the lower note to the upper one, both included: that is the number. Then count the half steps to tell the quality.
lesson.nudgeIntervalNumber: Count the letters from the lower note to the upper one, both included.
lesson.nudgeIntervalStep: Look at the piano keys between the two notes: is there one key between them, or none?
lesson.nudgeDegree: Count up the scale from its first note, one letter at a time, until you reach this note.
lesson.nudgeEarNote: Sing from the reference to the note, up or down, one step of the scale at a time, and count the steps.
lesson.nudgeEarInterval: Sing from the lower note to the upper one and count the half steps between them.
lesson.nudgeEarChord: Listen to the 3rd above the bass — bright or dark? — then to the 5th: steady, squeezed or stretched? Is there a fourth note on top?
lesson.nudgeEarScale: Sing it back slowly: where do the half steps fall, and is the 3rd above the first note bright or dark?
lesson.nudgeEarProgression: Hum the bass from chord to chord, and listen for the darker chords and for where the last one lands.
lesson.nudgeEarMelody: Trace the shape: does each note move up or down, by step or by leap? Then compare where each option ends.
lesson.oneTryNote: A question with only two options has one try.
